subtopic_detail: Suitability for planned VBAC per RANZCOG
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman at 36 plus 4 weeks in her third pregnancy at the antenatal clinic. Her first birth was an emergency caesarean at 38 weeks for foetal distress with a lower segment transverse incision. Her second birth was an uncomplicated VBAC at 40 weeks with a birthweight of 3.4 kg and no perineal trauma.

She has been counselled at earlier visits about mode of delivery options. She has a body mass index of 26. There is no previous uterine rupture, no previous classical caesarean, and no previous uterine perforation. Her current pregnancy has been uncomplicated with an anterior placenta.

Blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, no proteinuria, foetal fundal height corresponds to gestation, and cephalic presentation is confirmed by ultrasound today with an estimated foetal weight on the 50th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg; no proteinuria; foetal fundal height appropriate
data_table.Examination: Cephalic presentation confirmed on ultrasound; EFW 50th centile; anterior placenta
data_table.History: First birth emergency caesarean at 38 weeks for foetal distress (LSCS transverse); second birth uncomplicated VBAC at 40 weeks BW 3.4 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding mode of delivery?

options.text: Recommend a planned VBAC because prior successful VBAC substantially raises the chance of a successful subsequent VBAC and reduces the rupture risk in this labour
options.rationale: Prior successful VBAC increases the probability of subsequent VBAC to 85 to 90 percent and reduces uterine rupture rates to about 0.5 percent; RANZCOG supports planned VBAC in this scenario (Source: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section).
source_refs: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section

options.text: Recommend elective repeat caesarean at 39 weeks because any previous caesarean scar carries an unacceptable rupture risk with a subsequent labour and vaginal delivery attempt
options.rationale: A single previous lower segment transverse caesarean is not a contraindication to VBAC; a prior successful VBAC substantially reduces subsequent rupture risk to about 0.5 percent (Source: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section).
source_refs: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section

options.text: Recommend induction of labour with prostaglandin E2 vaginal pessary at 39 weeks because this shortens labour duration and reduces the risk of a subsequent emergency caesarean
options.rationale: Prostaglandin induction of labour after previous caesarean approximately triples uterine rupture risk and is generally avoided in favour of mechanical methods (balloon catheter) or spontaneous labour (Source: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section).
source_refs: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section

options.text: Recommend elective repeat caesarean because the interpregnancy interval is under 24 months and this substantially increases the risk of uterine rupture with a trial of labour in this pregnancy
options.rationale: Interpregnancy interval under 18 months is the accepted risk threshold; her previous VBAC was more than 2 years ago and interval is not the concern here (Source: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section).
source_refs: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section

options.text: Recommend home birth because her previous VBAC was uncomplicated and she is at very low risk of any labour complication warranting hospital based intrapartum monitoring and support
options.rationale: Planned VBAC should occur in a facility with continuous electronic foetal monitoring and immediate access to caesarean; home birth after previous caesarean is not supported by RANZCOG (Source: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section).
source_refs: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section

explanation.summary: RANZCOG supports planned vaginal birth after caesarean for women with a single previous lower segment transverse caesarean and no other contraindications. A prior successful VBAC increases the likelihood of a subsequent successful VBAC to 85 to 90 percent and reduces uterine rupture risk to about 0.5 percent. Contraindications include previous classical caesarean, previous uterine rupture, more than two previous caesareans, and placenta praevia. Induction with prostaglandins is generally avoided because it approximately triples rupture risk; mechanical induction or spontaneous labour is preferred.
key_points: Prior successful VBAC gives 85 to 90 percent success next time.
Rupture risk about 0.5 percent after prior successful VBAC.
Avoid prostaglandin induction because rupture risk is tripled.
explanation.pearls: Counsel women that planned VBAC requires continuous electronic foetal monitoring in labour and immediate access to emergency caesarean, so it is not appropriate for planned home birth or standalone birth centres.

sources.label: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section

subtopic_detail: Cervical priming decision using the Bishop score
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 34 year old primigravida on the antenatal ward at 41 plus 3 weeks admitted for post dates induction of labour. Her antenatal course has been uncomplicated. She has no medical comorbidities and body mass index at booking was 24. There is no known contraindication to vaginal delivery. The foetus is cephalic on ultrasound with an estimated weight of 3.6 kg.

On vaginal examination the cervix is posterior, 1 cm long, of firm consistency, and closed. The foetal head is 3 cm above the ischial spines. Membranes are intact.

Blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, foetal heart rate 138 bpm reactive on CTG. Bloods are within normal limits. Group B streptococcus screening at 36 weeks was negative. The team has discussed induction options with her and she has consented to the process being started today.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76 mmHg; foetal heart rate 138 bpm reactive
data_table.Examination: Cervix posterior; 1 cm long; firm; closed; head 3 cm above spines; membranes intact
data_table.Investigations: Bloods within normal limits; GBS screen negative
data_table.Obstetric: G1P0 at 41 plus 3 weeks; cephalic; EFW 3.6 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in induction of labour?

options.text: Perform artificial rupture of membranes now and commence a titrated intravenous oxytocin infusion 1 hour after the amniotomy is performed on the labour ward
options.rationale: An unripe cervix (Bishop score 1) is not suitable for amniotomy; cervical ripening is required first because forcing amniotomy risks failed induction and prolonged rupture of membranes (Source: RANZCOG Induction of labour statement).

options.text: Insert a Foley or double balloon transcervical catheter overnight for mechanical cervical priming and reassess the Bishop score in the morning after balloon removal
options.rationale: With a Bishop score of 1, mechanical cervical priming with a transcervical balloon (Foley or Cook double balloon) is a preferred first step and is safe for parous or nulliparous women (Source: RANZCOG Induction of labour statement).

options.text: Insert vaginal misoprostol 25 microg every 4 hours to a maximum of 4 doses over 24 hours and reassess the Bishop score after each dose before proceeding to amniotomy
options.rationale: Misoprostol is an acceptable ripening agent but at RANZCOG the standard prostaglandin option is dinoprostone; misoprostol dosing above 25 microg increases tachysystole and misoprostol is not the default first line agent (Source: RANZCOG Induction of labour statement).

options.text: Commence a titrated intravenous oxytocin infusion starting at 2 milliunits per minute now and increase every 30 minutes according to uterine contraction frequency and CTG trace
options.rationale: Oxytocin alone is not appropriate for cervical ripening with an unfavourable cervix; the risk of hyperstimulation and failed induction rises without priming (Source: RANZCOG Induction of labour statement).

options.text: Perform an urgent caesarean section today given that induction of labour with an unripe cervix is likely to fail and would expose her to prolonged labour and morbidity risk
options.rationale: Post dates induction with an unripe cervix is not itself a caesarean indication; success rates after mechanical priming and appropriate agents are high (Source: RANZCOG Induction of labour statement).

explanation.summary: The Bishop score summarises cervical readiness for induction across five features (position, length, consistency, dilatation, station). A score of 6 or less indicates an unripe cervix requiring priming before amniotomy or oxytocin. Options for priming are mechanical (Foley or Cook double balloon transcervical catheter) or prostaglandin (dinoprostone in Australia; misoprostol at low doses in selected settings). Amniotomy and oxytocin are appropriate first steps only when the cervix is favourable (Bishop score more than 6).
key_points: Bishop score 6 or less equals unripe cervix, needs priming.
Mechanical priming (Foley or Cook double balloon) is preferred first line.
Amniotomy and oxytocin follow when the cervix is favourable.
explanation.pearls: Mechanical balloon priming avoids uterine hyperstimulation risk associated with prostaglandins and is particularly useful in women with previous caesarean or in outpatient priming pathways.

subtopic_detail: First line uterotonic choice in atonic PPH with hypertension excluded
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 29 year old primigravida who delivered a 4.2 kg baby by normal vaginal delivery 20 minutes ago after a 90 minute second stage. The placenta was delivered by active management with intramuscular oxytocin at the delivery of the anterior shoulder and appeared complete. She has developed a heavy PV loss estimated at 1200 mL and ongoing.

On examination the uterus is boggy and above the umbilicus. There is no visible cervical tear on speculum inspection and the perineum has an intact second degree tear that has not been sutured. She has no history of hypertension, no known bleeding disorder, no drug allergies, and she did not have pre-eclampsia in this pregnancy.

Pulse rate 122/min, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C. Two large bore intravenous cannulae are in place. Group and hold is available and cross match has been sent. Baseline blood pressures throughout pregnancy were 105 to 115 systolic.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122/min; BP 88/52 mmHg; RR 24/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy above umbilicus; no cervical tear; second degree perineal tear unsutured; ongoing PV loss
data_table.Investigations: Group and hold available; cross match sent
data_table.Obstetric: Primigravida; NVD 20 min ago; baby 4.2 kg; second stage 90 min; active third stage with IM oxytocin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic?

options.text: Sublingual misoprostol 800 microg with continuous blood pressure monitoring and bimanual uterine compression while further intravenous access and blood products are being organised urgently
options.rationale: Misoprostol has slow onset compared to intramuscular ergometrine and is reserved for settings without access to injectable uterotonics; not first line in a hospital setting with ongoing loss (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 microg with continuous blood pressure monitoring and bimanual uterine compression while further intravenous access and blood products are being organised urgently
options.rationale: Carboprost is a third line uterotonic reserved for continued PPH despite oxytocin and ergometrine; jumping to it before ergometrine skips the standard sequence (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 microg with continuous blood pressure monitoring and bimanual uterine compression while further intravenous access and blood products are being organised urgently
options.rationale: Second line uterotonic after failed oxytocin in atonic PPH is intramuscular ergometrine 250 microg; her blood pressure is low so no contraindication exists, and bimanual compression is added mechanically (Source: RANZCOG PPH; AMH).

options.text: Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes with continuous blood pressure monitoring and bimanual uterine compression while further intravenous access and blood products are being organised urgently
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is given within 3 hours of onset as adjunct therapy but does not replace uterotonics; her uterus is atonic so uterotonic escalation is the priority (Source: WOMAN trial; RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 100 microg with continuous blood pressure monitoring and bimanual uterine compression while further intravenous access and blood products are being organised urgently
options.rationale: Adrenaline is not a uterotonic and has no role in atonic PPH; resuscitation should focus on blood products and directed uterotonics (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage).

explanation.summary: Atonic PPH is managed by simultaneous resuscitation and stepwise uterotonics. After failed initial oxytocin (IM at delivery of the anterior shoulder), the second line uterotonic is intramuscular ergometrine 250 microg unless the woman has hypertension or coronary disease. Third line is intramuscular carboprost 250 microg (avoid in asthma). Tranexamic acid is added within 3 hours as an adjunct per the WOMAN trial. Mechanical measures (bimanual compression, uterine balloon) run in parallel with uterotonic escalation.
key_points: Second line uterotonic is IM ergometrine 250 microg when no contraindication.
Third line is IM carboprost 250 microg; avoid in asthma.
TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours as adjunct per WOMAN trial.
explanation.pearls: Always call for help early, quantify blood loss with weighed swabs, and activate massive transfusion protocol before hypotension becomes refractory; PPH deaths are usually delays in escalation rather than absence of an available treatment.

subtopic_detail: Surgical management preference after prior contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman in the early pregnancy unit who has had a positive urine pregnancy test at home and now presents with right sided pelvic pain and light PV bleeding at an estimated 6 weeks by last menstrual period. She had a right sided salpingectomy 3 years ago for a ruptured right tubal ectopic pregnancy at a different hospital and has since had 12 months of unsuccessful natural conception attempts.

She has no dizziness, no shoulder tip pain, and no syncope. Her past history includes chlamydia treated 5 years ago and one previous laparoscopy for pelvic pain. She is haemodynamically stable and reports her left tube was described intraoperatively at the previous salpingectomy as macroscopically normal.

Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Serum beta HCG is 4600 IU/L today with a previous value of 4400 IU/L 48 hours ago. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with an endometrial thickness of 8 mm, an adnexal mass measuring 22 x 18 mm in the left tube containing a yolk sac and no visible cardiac activity, and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Haemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88/min; BP 118/74 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Mild right sided pelvic tenderness; no rebound; light PV bleeding on speculum
data_table.Investigations: Beta HCG 4600 IU/L today (from 4400 IU/L 48 h prior); TV US empty uterus; left tubal mass 22 x 18 mm with yolk sac no cardiac activity; no free fluid; Hb 128 g/L
data_table.History: G2P0 with prior right salpingectomy for ruptured ectopic; 12 months trying to conceive; chlamydia 5 years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre as a single dose today with weekly beta HCG monitoring until it falls below 15 IU/L on the standard early pregnancy unit pathway
options.rationale: Methotrexate is a reasonable option for haemodynamically stable ectopic with beta HCG under 5000 IU/L, no cardiac activity and no rupture, but her only remaining tube would be preserved by tubal surgery which is preferred here (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy; AMH).

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingectomy today because ectopic recurrence in the same tube is high and salpingectomy avoids the risk of persistent trophoblast and recurrent ectopic in the future
options.rationale: With a prior contralateral salpingectomy this is her only remaining tube; salpingectomy would leave her with no tubes and mandate IVF, so salpingostomy is preferred to preserve fertility (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy).

options.text: Expectant management with serial beta HCG measurements every 48 hours and repeat ultrasound weekly to allow the ectopic to resorb spontaneously without needing surgical or medical treatment
options.rationale: Expectant management requires beta HCG under 1000 IU/L and falling; her level is 4600 IU/L and rising, so expectant management is not appropriate here (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy).

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingostomy today with linear salpingostomy over the ectopic and weekly beta HCG monitoring to detect any persistent trophoblast that may need methotrexate rescue
options.rationale: With a prior contralateral salpingectomy this is her only remaining tube; salpingostomy preserves the tube and future fertility, with the trade off of monitoring for persistent trophoblast that may need methotrexate rescue (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy).

options.text: Laparotomy with left salpingectomy urgently today because there is a substantial risk of rupture in the next 24 hours given the size of the mass and the rising beta HCG level on serial testing
options.rationale: She is haemodynamically stable with no free fluid; laparoscopy is preferred over laparotomy, and salpingectomy in her only remaining tube commits her to IVF unnecessarily (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Choice between salpingectomy and salpingostomy for tubal ectopic pregnancy depends on the state of the contralateral tube. When the contralateral tube is healthy, salpingectomy is preferred because rates of persistent trophoblast and recurrent ectopic are lower and fertility outcomes are similar. When there is a prior contralateral salpingectomy or the contralateral tube is diseased, salpingostomy is preferred to preserve fertility, with the trade off of monitoring beta HCG weekly for persistent trophoblast that may require methotrexate rescue.
key_points: Healthy contralateral tube equals salpingectomy preferred.
Prior contralateral salpingectomy inverts to salpingostomy preferred.
Weekly beta HCG monitoring after salpingostomy to detect persistent trophoblast.
explanation.pearls: When the answer seems to obviously be the more definitive procedure (salpingectomy) in a stable patient, look for a prior contralateral surgical history that flips the standard answer; this is the T14 historical bilaterality inversion pattern.

subtopic_detail: Immediate first line manoeuvre in shoulder dystocia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to the birth suite for a suspected shoulder dystocia. A 30 year old multiparous woman at 39 plus 6 weeks has just delivered the foetal head after a normal vaginal delivery. The head has emerged but retracted against the perineum in a turtle sign after failure of restitution and no descent of the shoulders with routine axial traction on the next contraction.

Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated with a birthweight of 4.1 kg. This pregnancy has been complicated by well controlled gestational diabetes on diet alone. The estimated foetal weight at her 36 week ultrasound was on the 95th centile. Her BMI at booking was 32.

Foetal heart rate immediately before delivery of the head was 138 bpm. The midwife is at the woman's head; the birth suite senior midwife has entered the room. A time keeper has been designated and the paediatric team has been paged. There is no clinical evidence of maternal haemorrhage at this stage in the delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal stable; FHR 138 bpm immediately prior to delivery
data_table.Examination: Turtle sign after delivery of head; no descent with routine axial traction
data_table.Team: Time keeper set; senior midwife present; paediatric team paged
data_table.History: Multiparous; previous BW 4.1 kg; well controlled GDM diet only; EFW 95th centile at 36 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate first manoeuvre?

options.text: Deliberate posterior arm delivery by the accoucheur immediately after diagnosis; do not attempt McRoberts as it delays disimpaction of the anterior shoulder for the mother
options.rationale: Posterior arm delivery is an effective internal manoeuvre but is second line after McRoberts and suprapubic pressure; brachial plexus injury risk rises without prior external manoeuvres (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: Rubin II internal rotation manoeuvre by the accoucheur immediately after diagnosis; do not attempt McRoberts as it delays internal disimpaction of the anterior shoulder
options.rationale: Internal rotation manoeuvres are second line after McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail; jumping to them first misses the highest yield low morbidity first line intervention (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: Immediate deliberate cephalic replacement (Zavanelli manoeuvre) and preparation for a category 1 caesarean section by the obstetric consultant on call for the birth suite
options.rationale: Zavanelli manoeuvre is a last resort after HELPERR has failed; using it before McRoberts is not indicated and adds unnecessary morbidity (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: Fundal pressure applied by a second midwife on top of routine axial traction of the foetal head to encourage the anterior shoulder to slip beneath the pubic symphysis
options.rationale: Fundal pressure worsens shoulder impaction and increases risk of uterine rupture; it is explicitly contraindicated in shoulder dystocia (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: McRoberts manoeuvre with suprapubic pressure applied by an assistant immediately after positioning; continue axial traction on the foetal head with the next contraction
options.rationale: HELPERR sequence starts with McRoberts (hyperflexion of hips onto abdomen) plus suprapubic pressure; this resolves about 50 percent of shoulder dystocias and is the mandated first manoeuvre before internal manoeuvres (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia; ALSO).

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency requiring a fixed drill (HELPERR) after calling for help. The first manoeuvre is McRoberts (hyperflexion of the hips onto the abdomen) plus suprapubic pressure by an assistant; this resolves about 50 percent of cases. If unsuccessful, proceed to internal manoeuvres (Rubin II, Woods screw, posterior arm delivery). Fundal pressure is contraindicated. Zavanelli manoeuvre (cephalic replacement) is a last resort. Documentation with time keeping is essential and helps subsequent clinical governance and litigation defence.
key_points: First manoeuvre is McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure.
Fundal pressure is contraindicated.
Sequence: HELPERR - Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure suprapubic, Enter for internal, Remove posterior arm, Roll to all fours.
explanation.pearls: Time keeping starts at diagnosis of dystocia; the risk of hypoxic injury and brachial plexus injury rises after 5 minutes but many drills are completed in under 90 seconds if McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves the impaction quickly.

subtopic_detail: Delivery of the second twin after the first with a transverse lie and cord accessible
stem:
You are the senior obstetric registrar on the birth suite at a tertiary centre. A 34 year old primigravida with dichorionic diamniotic twins at 37 plus 3 weeks has just delivered twin 1 vaginally in a cephalic presentation with a birthweight of 2.7 kg after a straightforward labour and second stage.

Ultrasound in the birth suite immediately after delivery of twin 1 shows twin 2 in a transverse lie with the back downwards, an estimated foetal weight of 2.9 kg, and intact membranes. Cardiotocography of twin 2 is currently reactive at 140 bpm.

Maternal vital signs are stable; the woman is well analgesed with an epidural in situ. Consultants in obstetrics, anaesthetics and neonatology have been briefed antenatally regarding the intrapartum options and the woman has had a thorough discussion of them. The bladder is empty and the room is set up for both vaginal and operative delivery. No maternal or foetal contraindication to internal manoeuvres has been identified through her admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal stable; twin 2 FHR 140 bpm reactive
data_table.Examination: Twin 2 transverse lie with back down on ultrasound; membranes intact; EFW 2.9 kg; epidural in situ; bladder empty
data_table.Team: Obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatology briefed; consented intrapartum
data_table.Obstetric: G1P1 after delivery twin 1 cephalic 2.7 kg; DCDA twins 37 plus 3 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for the delivery of twin 2?

options.text: Perform internal podalic version of twin 2 to a footling breech followed by breech extraction under epidural anaesthesia with continuous cardiotocography and the neonatal team ready
options.rationale: For twin 2 in a transverse lie with a back down orientation, internal podalic version to a footling breech followed by breech extraction is the standard tertiary approach and is safer than caesarean of a second twin (Source: RANZCOG Management of twin pregnancy).

options.text: Perform external cephalic version of twin 2 to a cephalic presentation under continuous cardiotocography then amniotomy and titrated oxytocin augmentation to achieve vaginal delivery today
options.rationale: External cephalic version with a transverse back down lie and intact membranes has a low success rate and delays; internal podalic version and breech extraction has the highest success in this setting with an experienced accoucheur (Source: RANZCOG Management of twin pregnancy).

options.text: Perform an emergency category 1 caesarean section for twin 2 under general anaesthesia in view of the transverse lie and back down orientation and the risk of cord prolapse if membranes rupture
options.rationale: Caesarean of second twin after vaginal delivery of first twin carries significant maternal morbidity; internal podalic version and breech extraction avoids caesarean and has good foetal outcomes in experienced hands (Source: RANZCOG Management of twin pregnancy).

options.text: Perform artificial rupture of twin 2 membranes now and observe with continuous cardiotocography for spontaneous conversion to a longitudinal lie over the next 30 minutes with the woman on the bed
options.rationale: Rupturing membranes with a transverse lie risks cord prolapse and does not reliably convert to a longitudinal lie; membranes should be kept intact until the presenting part is engaged (Source: RANZCOG Management of twin pregnancy).

options.text: Perform amniotomy of twin 2 and immediate ventouse assisted vaginal delivery under continuous cardiotocography with the neonatal resuscitation team ready in the birth suite for the delivery
options.rationale: Ventouse assisted vaginal delivery is not possible for a transverse lie; the presenting part is not cephalic and instrumental delivery is not applicable to a non cephalic non longitudinal lie (Source: RANZCOG Management of twin pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Delivery of the second twin in transverse lie is best managed by internal podalic version followed by breech extraction when the accoucheur is experienced and the woman has been consented antenatally. External cephalic version has a low success rate in the intrapartum period and rupturing membranes with a transverse lie risks cord prolapse. Caesarean of the second twin after successful vaginal delivery of the first twin carries significant maternal morbidity and is reserved for cases where internal manoeuvres fail or are contraindicated.
key_points: Internal podalic version and breech extraction is preferred for transverse twin 2.
Keep membranes intact until presenting part is engaged.
Caesarean of twin 2 after vaginal delivery of twin 1 carries the highest maternal morbidity.
explanation.pearls: Success of internal podalic version and breech extraction depends on operator experience; twin delivery drills at tertiary centres include simulation training for this specific manoeuvre and both consultant obstetrician and anaesthetist should be at the bedside from delivery of twin 1.

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant choice in a breastfeeding mother with moderate MDD postpartum
stem:
You are the perinatal mental health registrar reviewing a 31 year old woman 8 weeks post partum with her first baby. She had a history of a single depressive episode in her early twenties that resolved without medication. She is exclusively breastfeeding and her infant is thriving. Her partner is available in the home most of the time and her mother has been staying with the family for the past week.

Over the last 3 weeks she has developed persistent low mood, anhedonia with her baby, poor sleep even when the baby sleeps, poor appetite with a 2 kg weight loss, and feelings of guilt that she is not bonding with her baby. She has no thoughts of harming herself or the baby but is tearful daily. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is 18 today. She has no obsessional intrusive thoughts and no perceptual disturbance.

She has no history of bipolar disorder, no family history of psychosis, and no other medications. She is asking about starting an antidepressant.

data_table.Examination: Tearful, congruent affect; no psychotic features; no obsessional intrusive thoughts
data_table.Screening: EPDS 18; no suicidal ideation; no infanticidal ideation
data_table.History: First baby 8 weeks post partum; exclusively breastfeeding; single depressive episode age twenties resolved untreated; no bipolar; no other medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological plan?

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily with routine perinatal follow up in 2 weeks to review response, tolerability, and infant behaviour on this regimen for postnatal depression today
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a long half life and higher relative infant dose than sertraline (about 5 to 9 percent); it accumulates in breastfed infants and is not preferred first line in this setting (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline; AMH).

options.text: Sertraline 25 mg orally daily for 7 days then 50 mg daily with routine perinatal follow up in 2 weeks to review response, tolerability, and infant behaviour on this regimen
options.rationale: Sertraline has the lowest relative infant dose (about 0.5 percent) among SSRIs and is the preferred first line antidepressant in breastfeeding mothers; starting low and titrating minimises adverse effects (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline; AMH).

options.text: Paroxetine 20 mg orally daily with routine perinatal follow up in 2 weeks to review response, tolerability, and infant behaviour on this regimen for postnatal depression today
options.rationale: Paroxetine transfers to breast milk in low quantities but has significant discontinuation and anticholinergic side effects; sertraline is preferred first line in breastfeeding (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline; AMH).

options.text: Venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily with routine perinatal follow up in 2 weeks to review response, tolerability, and infant behaviour on this regimen for postnatal depression today
options.rationale: SNRIs like venlafaxine are second line in perinatal setting; discontinuation symptoms and elevated blood pressure limit their first line use over sertraline (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline).

options.text: Amitriptyline 25 mg orally at night with routine perinatal follow up in 2 weeks to review response, tolerability, and infant behaviour on this regimen for postnatal depression today
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants have overdose lethality and anticholinergic effects that make them non first line; sertraline is safer in this population (Source: RANZCP perinatal guideline; AMH).

explanation.summary: Postnatal depression at 8 weeks with an Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale of 13 or higher and functional impairment warrants active treatment. First line pharmacotherapy in a breastfeeding mother is sertraline because of its lowest relative infant dose among SSRIs (about 0.5 percent) and reassuring longitudinal safety data. Fluoxetine and paroxetine are not first line: fluoxetine because of long half life accumulation in the infant, paroxetine because of discontinuation effects. Psychological therapy (CBT or IPT) is added alongside pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Sertraline is first line SSRI in breastfeeding.
Fluoxetine avoided due to long half life and infant accumulation.
Combine with psychological therapy for best outcomes.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about intrusive obsessional thoughts of harming the baby; obsessive compulsive disorder frequently first presents in the postnatal period and may be under recognised because women fear disclosure will trigger child protection involvement.

stem:
You are the general adult psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34 year old man in outpatient clinic with newly diagnosed bipolar I disorder after a first manic episode 6 weeks ago. He was stabilised as an inpatient with olanzapine 10 mg orally at night and is now euthymic. Discharge plan was to commence a mood stabiliser at the first outpatient appointment.

He has no significant medical history, has never had a seizure, has no cardiac disease, has no thyroid disease, and does not drink alcohol. He is not currently sexually active with anyone who could become pregnant. He is medication compliant and understands the diagnosis.

Blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, weight 78 kg, body mass index 24. He has agreed to a trial of lithium after informed discussion with his treating consultant and after receiving the RANZCP lithium information sheet at his previous outpatient appointment.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic; no tremor; no thyroid enlargement
data_table.History: First manic episode 6 weeks ago; olanzapine 10 mg nocte; no medical comorbidities; RANZCP information sheet provided
data_table.Consent: Informed discussion completed; agreed to trial of lithium

lead_in: Which set of baseline investigations is most appropriate before commencing lithium?

options.text: Urea electrolytes creatinine; thyroid function tests; liver function tests; fasting lipids; fasting glucose; and a 12 lead ECG plus an echocardiogram to assess baseline ventricular function
options.rationale: Liver function is not lithium relevant (renally excreted) and echocardiogram is not routine baseline; this bundle overtests without adding lithium safety information (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

options.text: Urea electrolytes creatinine; thyroid function tests; a 24 hour urine collection for creatinine clearance; full blood count; and lipids including fasting cholesterol and triglycerides
options.rationale: 24 hour urine creatinine clearance is not needed baseline; eGFR from serum creatinine is standard and 24 hour collection is reserved for CKD monitoring or when eGFR is discordant with clinical picture (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

options.text: Urea electrolytes and creatinine; thyroid function tests; calcium; full blood count; beta HCG for people who could become pregnant; and a 12 lead ECG
options.rationale: Standard baseline before lithium includes renal function (UEC), thyroid function, calcium (parathyroid effect), FBC, pregnancy testing where relevant, and ECG in patients over 40 or with cardiac risk factors; this covers organs lithium can affect (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline; AMH).

options.text: Urea electrolytes creatinine; thyroid function tests; parathyroid hormone; vitamin D; magnesium; and phosphate levels prior to commencing therapy today
options.rationale: Parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and phosphate are not routine baseline; calcium is measured as a proxy for parathyroid effect and PTH is checked only if calcium is high (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

options.text: Urea electrolytes creatinine; thyroid function tests; full blood count; and a plain chest x ray to establish baseline pulmonary status before commencement of the medication
options.rationale: Chest x ray is not part of lithium baseline; calcium and ECG (in over 40 or with cardiac risk) are the necessary additions to renal and thyroid function testing (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

explanation.summary: Baseline investigations before commencing lithium target the organs lithium can affect over time: kidney (UEC and eGFR), thyroid, parathyroid (measured via corrected calcium), and cardiac conduction (ECG in patients over 40 or with cardiac risk factors). Beta HCG is done in people who could become pregnant because lithium is associated with Ebstein anomaly at first trimester exposure. A full blood count is baseline for benign leucocytosis. Ongoing monitoring is 6 monthly UEC, TFTs and calcium with lithium levels 12 hours post dose at week 1, week 2, and any dose change.
key_points: Baseline: UEC, TFT, calcium, FBC, beta HCG if applicable, ECG.
Monitoring: 6 monthly UEC, TFT, calcium; lithium level 12 h post dose.
Target therapeutic level 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L in maintenance; 0.8 to 1.0 in acute mania.
explanation.pearls: Warn the patient about NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides, which reduce lithium clearance; dehydration from vomiting, diarrhoea or heat exposure is a common trigger for lithium toxicity and warrants a same day lithium level and hold.

subtopic_detail: Baseline and monitoring requirements before clozapine commencement
stem:
You are the consultation psychiatry registrar reviewing a 28 year old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia in the community mental health team. He has failed adequate trials of two antipsychotics (risperidone up to 6 mg daily for 8 weeks and olanzapine up to 20 mg daily for 8 weeks) at adequate doses with confirmed adherence via depot dispensing.

He continues to experience persistent auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions and remains functionally impaired. He agrees to a trial of clozapine after informed discussion. He has no personal or family history of blood dyscrasia and no cardiac disease. His baseline BMI is 26.

Blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, pulse rate 82/min. Baseline blood tests before commencing clozapine include full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, liver function tests, fasting glucose, lipids, HbA1c, high sensitivity troponin, and a 12 lead ECG plus a transthoracic echocardiogram.

data_table.Investigations: FBC; UEC; LFT; fasting glucose; lipids; HbA1c; high sensitivity troponin; ECG; TTE
data_table.History: Treatment resistant schizophrenia; failed adequate trials of risperidone and olanzapine; no blood dyscrasia; no cardiac disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate haematological monitoring plan for the first 18 weeks of clozapine?

options.text: Monthly full blood count for the first 18 weeks then 3 monthly thereafter and register with the manufacturer clozapine patient monitoring service for ongoing safety monitoring after commencement
options.rationale: Monthly monitoring is inadequate for the first 18 weeks when agranulocytosis risk is highest; weekly is mandated (Source: AMH; RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

options.text: Weekly full blood count for the first 4 weeks then monthly thereafter and register with the manufacturer clozapine patient monitoring service for ongoing safety monitoring after commencement
options.rationale: Weekly monitoring extends to 18 weeks because agranulocytosis risk is highest in the first 18 weeks; stopping weekly at 4 weeks misses the risk window (Source: AMH).

options.text: Fortnightly full blood count for the first 18 weeks then monthly thereafter and register with the manufacturer clozapine patient monitoring service for ongoing safety monitoring after commencement
options.rationale: Weekly rather than fortnightly monitoring is required for the first 18 weeks because agranulocytosis risk is dose independent and time dependent (Source: AMH; RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

options.text: Weekly full blood count for the first 18 weeks then fortnightly to 12 months then monthly thereafter and register with the manufacturer clozapine patient monitoring service
options.rationale: AMH and RANZCP clozapine monitoring requires weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks (highest agranulocytosis risk), fortnightly to 12 months, then monthly for life with registration on the manufacturer monitoring service (Source: AMH; RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

options.text: Weekly full blood count for the first 6 weeks then fortnightly for 6 weeks then monthly thereafter with registration on the manufacturer clozapine patient monitoring service program
options.rationale: This schedule does not match the AMH mandated protocol; weekly for 18 weeks then fortnightly to 12 months then monthly is the correct protocol (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Clozapine agranulocytosis risk is highest in the first 18 weeks of therapy (about 0.8 percent lifetime risk overall). Australian monitoring per AMH and the RANZCP schizophrenia guideline is weekly full blood count for the first 18 weeks, fortnightly to 12 months, then monthly for life. Patient and prescriber must be registered on the manufacturer clozapine patient monitoring service. Additional monitoring includes weekly troponin and CRP for the first 4 weeks for myocarditis, and 3 monthly metabolic monitoring (weight, lipids, HbA1c).
key_points: Weekly FBC for 18 weeks then fortnightly to 12 months then monthly for life.
Weekly troponin and CRP for first 4 weeks to detect myocarditis.
Register both patient and prescriber on the manufacturer monitoring service.
explanation.pearls: Any interruption of clozapine over 48 hours mandates retitration from the starting dose because postural hypotension and sedation return rapidly; check the reset protocol before restart rather than resuming the previous dose.

subtopic_detail: Discriminating neuroleptic malignant syndrome from serotonin syndrome
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 42 year old man with schizoaffective disorder brought in by his partner with 24 hours of confusion, fever and rigidity. He was commenced on haloperidol 5 mg orally twice daily one week ago after presenting to community mental health with a psychotic exacerbation. He has been on paroxetine 40 mg orally daily for the last 2 years for comorbid major depressive disorder.

He has no illicit drug use, has not taken tramadol or any triptans, and has not had linezolid or MAOIs. His partner reports he seemed sedated over the past 3 days rather than agitated and that he has not been drinking much water.

Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 158/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 39.6 degrees C. On examination he has lead pipe rigidity in all four limbs, hyporeflexia, no clonus, and marked diffuse sweating. Creatine kinase is 8600 U/L (less than 200), white cell count is 14 x10^9/L, sodium is 148 mmol/L, and creatinine is 148 micromol/L (baseline 82 micromol/L).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min; BP 158/98 mmHg; RR 22/min; SpO2 97% RA; T 39.6 C
data_table.Examination: Confused; lead pipe rigidity all four limbs; hyporeflexia; no clonus; diffuse sweating; mute
data_table.Investigations: CK 8600 U/L; WCC 14 x10^9/L; sodium 148 mmol/L; creatinine 148 (baseline 82); pH 7.34; lactate 2.1 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Haloperidol 5 mg BD started 1 week ago; paroxetine 40 mg daily 2 years; no MAOI, no tramadol, no triptan, no illicit

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Serotonin syndrome secondary to paroxetine with an interaction from the dopamine blockade of haloperidol producing an atypical presentation of the syndrome with fever and rigidity
options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome features neuromuscular hyperactivity with hyperreflexia, clonus (especially lower limbs) and shivering; this patient has hyporeflexia, no clonus and lead pipe rigidity, which is the NMS pattern (Source: Sternbach; Hunter criteria).

options.text: Encephalitis with autonomic dysregulation secondary to a viral prodrome with new confusion, fever, and creatinine rise; the movement disorder is a non specific accompaniment of the systemic infection
options.rationale: There is a clear temporal association with commencement of haloperidol and a classic NMS syndrome (rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, elevated creatine kinase); encephalitis would not usually produce lead pipe rigidity and elevated creatine kinase (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

options.text: Malignant hyperthermia secondary to a preceding halogenated anaesthetic exposure with severe hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, elevated creatine kinase, and marked metabolic acidosis on arterial gas analysis
options.rationale: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anaesthetics or suxamethonium; there is no anaesthetic exposure in this history so the diagnosis does not fit (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

options.text: Anticholinergic toxicity secondary to the anticholinergic burden of high dose haloperidol producing dry skin, urinary retention, tachycardia, hyperthermia, and altered mental state as classic features today
options.rationale: Anticholinergic toxicity produces dry skin (not diffuse sweating), mydriasis, and urinary retention without rigidity or elevated creatine kinase; the sweating and rigidity here argues against it (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome secondary to recent commencement of haloperidol; hyporeflexia, lead pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability and elevated creatine kinase support the diagnosis today
options.rationale: NMS presents with lead pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia (not hyperreflexia), hyperthermia, autonomic instability and elevated creatine kinase within 1 to 2 weeks of starting a dopamine antagonist; his picture fits Levenson and DSM 5 TR criteria (Source: Sternbach; RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

explanation.summary: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin syndrome can present with hyperthermia, altered mental state and autonomic instability but are discriminated by the neuromuscular examination. NMS presents with lead pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, mutism and bradykinesia within 1 to 2 weeks of starting or increasing a dopamine antagonist. Serotonin syndrome presents with neuromuscular hyperactivity: hyperreflexia, clonus (especially lower limbs), shivering, and myoclonus within 24 hours of a serotonergic agent change. Creatine kinase is typically higher in NMS.
key_points: NMS: lead pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, high CK, dopamine antagonist trigger.
Serotonin syndrome: hyperreflexia, clonus, shivering, serotonergic trigger.
Onset: NMS days to weeks; serotonin syndrome hours.
explanation.pearls: Management of NMS is stop the antipsychotic, aggressive cooling, IV fluid resuscitation to protect against rhabdomyolysis induced acute kidney injury, and dantrolene or bromocriptine in refractory cases; ECT is considered for prolonged severe cases.
